items.title: [pewresearch.org] Pew projects Muslims will surpass Christians globally by 2035
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Muslims are projected to become the world’s largest religious group by 2035, reaching 2.57 billion people compared with 2.52 billion Christians, according to new projections from the Pew Research Center. Both populations are expected to grow, but the Muslim population is projected to increase faster, mainly because Muslim women had an average of 3.1 children in 2020-2025, compared with 2.5 among Christian women. Pew estimates there were 2.02 billion Muslims and 2.27 billion Christians in 2020. If current trends continue, the Muslim population will exceed 3.6 billion by 2070, while the Christian population will remain just below 3 billion. The world population is projected to grow 29% over the same period. The report models demographic patterns across 201 countries and territories, including age, fertility, mortality, migration and religious switching. Its projections do not account for events such as wars, epidemics or natural disasters. By 2070, sub-Saharan Africa is expected to be home to more than half of the world’s Christians, while Pakistan is projected to have the largest Muslim population. Pew’s researchers say the projected growth is largely taking place in countries where each faith is already predominant, rather than reflecting a direct shift from one religion to the other.

items.title: [elpais.com] Journalist's murder in Costa Rica raises alarm among regional press
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Costa Rican journalist Camilo Rodríguez Chaverri was shot dead on November 16, three days after an unknown person set fire to two cars and part of the home of Panamanian investigative journalist Rolando Rodríguez in Panama City. Following the killing in Santo Domingo de Heredia, Costa Rica, press organizations and the United Nations called for an investigation and warned of its chilling effect on journalism. Reporters Without Borders (RSF), an international organization that defends press freedom, said it had already raised the alarm about pressure on critical journalists and obstacles to reporting independently. A University of Costa Rica poll published on November 11 found that 58% of the population considers journalism dangerous to practice, and 54.7% believes freedom of expression is at risk. The Costa Rican Prosecutor's Office said it would examine Rodríguez's public allegations, the people he named, and other possible motives for the crime. It added that it seeks to identify both the perpetrators and those who ordered the killing. President Laura Fernández condemned the murder and said she had ordered the police forces to cooperate with the investigation.

items.title: [nasa.gov] Voyager 1 stops sending science data before one-light-day milestone
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

NASA’s Voyager 1 has stopped sending science and engineering data, though its carrier signal remains detectable, the agency said as it confirmed the spacecraft reached one light-day from Earth on Nov. 18. Launched in 1977, the probe is now more than 16 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers) away in interstellar space; its signal took 24 hours to reach Earth. The spacecraft has sent no data since Nov. 14. Engineers are investigating the fault. NASA said a similar interruption in 2023 was traced to an onboard computer, while the current issue may also involve the computer that collects and formats instrument readings. The carrier signal shows the spacecraft is still transmitting and allowed engineers to verify its distance, but it does not provide the missing science readings. Voyager project manager Suzanne Dodd said the team remains in contact with the probe. Because signals take a day each way, sending a command and receiving a response now takes about two days, slowing efforts to diagnose the fault and restore the data flow.

items.title: [space.com] Apollo 12 lightning strikes prompted NASA to tighten launch weather rules
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Lightning struck NASA’s Apollo 12 Saturn V rocket twice within seconds of its Nov. 14, 1969, launch, disrupting spacecraft telemetry and endangering the mission. Mission Control engineer John Aaron recognized the readings from an earlier test and recommended switching the Signal Conditioning Equipment to its auxiliary setting, which restored the data. Investigators concluded the rocket and its conductive exhaust plume had triggered a discharge in an electrically charged part of the atmosphere, even though no active thunderstorm lay along the immediate flight path. NASA expanded launch weather restrictions to account for atmospheric electrical conditions, not only visible lightning and thunderstorms.

items.title: [livescience.com] Four Guangxi fossil teeth point to Denisovans and another ancient lineage
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Researchers analyzing four fossil teeth from two caves in China’s Guangxi region identified Denisovan-related remains and evidence of a potentially distinct ancient human lineage, according to a study published in Nature on Nov. 25. The two Longchuandong teeth align with Denisovans, while two teeth from Chuanshandong—at least 100,800 years old—have traits that do not readily match any known East Asian Homo group. The findings suggest different archaic human populations lived in southern China during overlapping periods, but researchers cannot yet confidently assign the Chuanshandong teeth to a named group. Warm, humid conditions in the region hinder ancient DNA preservation, so researchers analyzed tooth shape and proteins. They say more fossils and molecular evidence are needed to establish the teeth’s evolutionary relationships.

items.title: [ft.com] UK tribunal orders disclosure of secret Apple data-access notice
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

The UK Investigatory Powers Tribunal ruled on Nov. 19 that the government could not keep secret a notice requiring Apple to give authorities access to encrypted customer data. The Home Office acknowledged issuing it. The judges rejected the claim that confirming the notice would harm national security, saying the government had not established that risk. The ruling addresses disclosure, not whether the government has the legal power to make the demand or what technical changes it requires. Those details remain secret, and a substantive hearing is expected in 2027. The dispute began with a January 2025 demand for access to users’ data worldwide, which Britain later withdrew after negotiations with the Trump administration. A second notice, issued in July 2026 and reportedly limited to UK customers, prompted Apple’s renewed challenge. Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge says the company’s Claude assistant helped him prove the Riemann hypothesis, a longstanding mathematical claim about prime-number distribution. The claimed proof remains subject to human verification. Johns Hopkins University’s mathematics department has issued guidance for Ph.D. applicants and job candidates, saying it expects transparency about AI use and will not give written work positive weight unless candidates demonstrate they understand it. Professor Yiannis Sakellaridis said the guidance was prompted by the risk that candidates could submit AI-generated proofs without learning the underlying mathematics, not by a specific applicant case. Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei rejected the idea that people should hand governance to AI, while David Krueger, founder of the nonprofit Evitable, argued that concern about losing control calls for a halt to advanced AI development. Researchers and technology leaders have debated whether the mathematical advances signal progress toward systems that exceed human capabilities.

items.title: [nacion.com] Latin American countries raise the alarm over rising diabetes rates and underdiagnosis
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Health figures released for World Diabetes Day show diagnoses and undetected cases in several Latin American countries. Costa Rica reported 17,276 diagnoses in 2025, 28.62% more than in 2024; in Panama, the Social Security Fund treated around 53,000 people during 2025, while an estimated 312,800 adults were living with diabetes in 2024. In Mexico, more than 14 million adults have the disease, and nearly one in three is unaware of their diagnosis. National estimates do not necessarily use the same methods. In Brazil, an estimated five million people remain undiagnosed, in addition to the 16 million who have been diagnosed. In Argentina, nearly four in 10 people with abnormal test results were unaware of their condition. The International Diabetes Federation estimates that more than 589 million adults worldwide are living with diabetes. Type 2 diabetes can progress for years without clear symptoms; when blood glucose remains high, it can cause cardiovascular, kidney, vision, and nerve damage. Authorities and specialists recommend screening tests, clinical follow-up, and sustained lifestyle changes. Costa Rica recorded another 16,758 new cases up to the epidemiological week of October 18–24, 2026.

items.title: [Macworld] How accurately does the Apple Watch measure your heart rate? We put it to the test
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Macworld

With the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, Apple introduced a new health-sensing system. The new energy-efficient LED sensors measure heart rate every five seconds. Heart rate variability is also measured significantly more frequently than before. Macwelt was able to verify this in our review of the Apple Watch Series 12. The watch now measures your pulse every five seconds even when you’re not exercising, and heart rate variability is now recorded every five minutes. The battery still lasts for 24 hours.

This is exciting, because the Apple Watch already had stellar heart-rate tracking. How often and how accurately has the Apple Watch been measuring key health parameters to date? Apple hides the answers to these questions in its support documents. For some measurements, there are no official figures at all. So we took a closer look using the Apple Watch Series 11, which has the same third-gen optical heart rate sensor that was introduced with the Apple Watch Series 6.

How often does the Apple Watch Series 11 measure heart rate?

The answer to this question depends on the situation and the settings on your Apple Watch. In workout mode, the Apple Watch measures your heart rate every five seconds. The watch also measures your heart rate at this high frequency for the first three minutes after your workout. However, there is also a special setting for long workouts, where the user can activate power-saving mode if required. Apple claims that measurements are taken less frequently in this mode. I recorded a HIIT workout using the Polar H10 chest strap as a reference device. I also started the same workout on the Apple Watch Series 11.

Foundry

The Apple Watch actually measures heart rate every five seconds while the wearer is exercising. Measurements in power-saving mode during a workout also take place every five seconds. However, the system pauses the measurement for several minutes. This means that the heart rate is measured in short intervals every 5 seconds, then the Apple Watch pauses. You can see this on the graph of the heart rates measured during the workout up to the green line: up to that point, the Apple Watch was running in power-saving mode; after that, I switched it off.

Speaking of power-saving mode. If this mode is activated all the time, no background measurements take place, neither of the heart rate nor of heart rate variability. Furthermore, the vital signs data following a recorded night’s sleep lacks the oxygen saturation readings from during the night.

The Apple Watch can also measure your heart rate every second, just like chest straps do during a workout. However, these measurements only occur sporadically: during user-initiated ECG readings and during background HRV measurements. When you launch the ECG app and place your finger on the Digital Crown, the animation on the Watch and the PDF generated afterwards show the heart rate readings for every second. During HRV measurement, too, the Apple Watch records each heart rate over the course of a minute and then uses a specific formula to calculate the time interval between individual heartbeats.

In the background, and particularly at night while you’re asleep, the Apple Watch measures your heart rate every five minutes. However, the measurements aren’t as regular as they are during exercise. The intervals can vary more significantly when you’re at rest.

I exported and analysed measurements from a sample night using the Health app. For the sake of clarity, the chart above shows only one hour. During six and a half hours of sleep, the Apple Watch took 83 measurements. The average interval between measurements here is 4 minutes 39 seconds, although gaps of 16 minutes or as little as 40 seconds are also possible.

How accurately does the Apple Watch measure heart rate data?

When unveiling the Apple Watch Series 12, Apple claimed that the new smartwatch was the most accurate heart rate fitness tracker on the market. While we can only verify this claim through a single test, older models show that the Apple Watch was already quite accurate when it came to heart rate measurement.

When we tested the Apple Watch Ultra 3, we found that the Ultra’s readings deviated only very slightly from those of the chest strap. I analysed the same HIIT workout described above using the Apple Watch Series 11. The following picture emerges from the progression of the two graphs. On average, the Apple Watch measures your heart rate quite accurately during exercise.

The correlation coefficient between the two measurements–from the Polar H10 and the Apple Watch Series 11–is 0.95. This means the Apple Watch measures quite closely to a chest strap. On average, the two readings differ by just one beat. However, there are outliers: the higher the heart rate, the less accurate the measurement becomes. This can be seen in the line showing heart rates of 160 beats per minute and above. The measurement is also rather inaccurate in power-saving mode, as the Apple Watch can completely miss heart rate spikes due to the sporadic mode.

The new features Apple announced for the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 are exciting because they effectively turn the entire heart rate measurement algorithm on its head.

items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Switzerland’s National Cyber Security Centre says attackers using AI agents breached systems in four of five cases reported in the country, including attacks on three critical-infrastructure operators. The cases are part of a rise in campaigns using AI frameworks to automate reconnaissance and exploit security weaknesses. The Swiss agency has not identified the attackers, and officials reported no major outages. Italy’s incident response team says it observed campaigns in which multiple agents worked in parallel to compromise exposed systems. Canada’s cyber centre says automated tools have shortened some reconnaissance and exploitation from days or weeks to minutes. Amazon separately described agents that found and exploited an unpatched flaw on a university server in about 11 minutes. Swiss authorities advise organizations to reduce the number of internet-facing systems and install critical updates within 24 hours of release. Italy also urged operators to restrict remote-management access and monitor unusual authentication and network activity.

items.title: [cyberscoop.com] Kazakh ransomware suspect extradited to US in healthcare extortion case
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Kazakh national Roman Khlynovskiy, 43, was extradited from Italy and appeared in federal court in Knoxville, Tennessee, on charges related to alleged ransomware attacks on U.S. hospitals, schools and healthcare providers. Prosecutors say he was part of the 8-Digits Team, a group linked to the INC and Lynx ransomware operations that breached networks, stole data and demanded payment not to publish it. The indictment says the group claimed to possess more than 50 terabytes of stolen data, including over 70 million confidential health records, and issued ransom demands totaling more than $500 million. Khlynovskiy faces charges including computer fraud, wire fraud, extortion and money laundering, as well as threats involving nonconsensual intimate images under the TAKE IT DOWN Act. If convicted on all charges, he could face up to 27 years in prison. The FBI said its investigation is continuing.

The Council of the European Union and the European Parliament reached a provisional agreement on Nov. 18 to speed up permitting for renewable energy projects, electricity grids and storage facilities, aiming to reduce construction delays and strengthen energy security. The changes also cover recharging stations and authorizations for new electricity and gas infrastructure. items.title: [krdo.com] Investigators suspect AI tool in breach of three US spy agencies
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

U.S. investigators suspect hackers used Artex, an AI-enabled penetration-testing framework, to breach an unclassified intelligence-analysis system used by the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA), the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI) and the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency (NGA). Early indicators point to China, but no attacker has been publicly identified. The network processes open-source intelligence, and officials have said classified information was not compromised. The network combines publicly available material with commercially sourced datasets, social-media content and satellite imagery. Investigators have not specified what records were accessed or when the breach occurred. An ODNI official said critical capabilities and classified systems were not disrupted, and a person familiar with the incident told The Associated Press the issue had been resolved. Separately, the Treasury Department’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) disclosed that it was investigating unauthorized access to a limited subset of its systems. The agency took some systems offline as a precaution, directed banks to use its Financial Institutions Hotline for reports, and said the FBI, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) and outside forensic examiners were assessing the incident.

items.title: [theregister.com] Web-testing platform Optimizely breach exposes visitors at 178 sites to malware
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Hackers exploited a vulnerability in website-testing platform Optimizely on Nov. 16, injecting malicious JavaScript into scripts used by 178 organizations, including the BBC, CNN, Zoom, IKEA, HSBC and Salesforce. Security researcher Scott Helme and cybersecurity firm Report URI found that the code reached visitors through Optimizely’s trusted delivery infrastructure, without requiring attackers to break into each customer’s servers. The scripts attempted to replace cryptocurrency wallet addresses, capture card details entered into website forms, steal browser cookies, take screenshots and load exploit kits targeting older Apple iPhones and iPads. Report URI tracked about $7,040 in cryptocurrency sent to attacker-linked wallets in roughly nine hours. Researchers could not establish how many card details were stolen and reported no confirmed iPhone takeover in this campaign. Optimizely said it patched the flaw, removed the injected code, revoked tokens and reset access for affected accounts. Salesforce disabled the scripts while investigating, and IKEA opened an inquiry. Equifax stopped using the service and said it found no evidence its systems were compromised.

Lebanon’s National News Agency reported that the strike hit the Al-Shaara area at dawn and caused no casualties or damage. The Israeli military also said it detained two men in southern Lebanon whom it described as Hezbollah-guided operatives; Lebanese state media said Israeli forces seized two brothers in Shebaa. A U.S.-backed framework for Lebanon calls for Hezbollah’s disarmament, an Israeli troop withdrawal and Lebanese army deployment in the south, but implementation has stalled and Hezbollah has rejected surrendering its weapons. Haaretz described the attack as a departure from Israel’s prolonged restraint on strikes deep inside Lebanon. Israeli forces continue operating in a self-declared security zone along the border.

Perspective: Israeli military: It said the shipment was intended to strengthen Hezbollah’s ability to attack Israeli civilians and soldiers. It said it would continue operations to remove threats while remaining committed to the ceasefire (albawaba.com, jpost.com). (Al Bawaba)
Perspective: Hezbollah lawmakers: They have maintained that the group is rebuilding its military capabilities while rejecting the government’s disarmament decision and direct negotiations with Israel under U.S. sponsorship (aawsat.com).
Quote: "Hezbollah will disarm. They should do that voluntarily." (Mike Waltz, U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, The Jerusalem Post)
Timeline: June 2026: U.S.-mediated Israel-Lebanon framework set out security arrangements (ahram.org.eg)
Timeline: 4 August 2026: Lebanese army seized Grad rockets and arrested two suspected smugglers (enabbaladi.net)
Timeline: 5 November 2026: Israeli military said it found more than 340 weapons (jpost.com)
Timeline: 16 November 2026: Israel struck the Janta area and claimed it targeted an arms shipment (aawsat.com, jpost.com)
Background: Hezbollah fought two successive wars with Israel from 2023 onward, losing senior leaders and part of its arsenal (aawsat.com). The ouster of Syrian President Bashar al-Assad in late 2024 cut off a major weapons-supply route for Hezbollah (aawsat.com).
